article.Citation: Davis AK, Barsuglia JP, Windham-Herman AM, Lynch M, Polanco M. Subjective effectiveness of ibogaine treatment for problematic opioid consumption: Short- and long-term outcomes and current psychological functioning. Journal of Psychedelic Studies. 2017.
article.Title: Subjective effectiveness of ibogaine treatment for problematic opioid consumption: Short- and long-term outcomes and current psychological functioning
article.GenderCategory: male/female (73% male, 27% female); no non-binary/other categories reported

ae_events.Description: 74% of participants endorsed experiencing physical discomfort during ibogaine treatment; no detail on nature, duration, or clinical management given.
51% endorsed experiencing fear during the ibogaine session; expected challenging-experience phenomenology with no reported intervention or lasting impairment.
49% endorsed seeing frightening images during the ibogaine session; in-session perceptual challenging experience, no further detail reported.
36% endorsed recalling and experiencing difficult memories from their past during the ibogaine session; no detail on distress or duration.

article.IsObservational: Retrospective, anonymous, cross-sectional web-based survey of individuals who received ibogaine treatment in usual clinical care at a single Mexico facility (2012-2015); no randomization or controlled experimental arms — naturalistic observational/survey design consistent with corpus curation.
article.Substance: Primary tracked intervention is ibogaine hydrochloride. Authors disclose that Crossroads' clinical procedures changed partway through the 2012-2015 window to add 5-MeO-DMT following ibogaine for some patients, but could not determine with certainty which participants received it (anonymous survey, recall/design error) and could not formally analyze its effect (exploratory date-based analysis found no significant difference). Coded Substance as Ibogaine only since that is the formally tracked intervention; 5-MeO-DMT is a disclosed but unquantifiable confound, not a coded arm.
article.N: N=88 is the final analyzed sample after excluding 33 people who did not complete the main questionnaires and 13 who sought ibogaine for non-opioid substance problems, out of 134 who began the survey and 285 contacted.
article.AE_denominator: Table 2 subjective-effects percentages are reported for the 'Full sample' column (n=88, i.e., 68 responders + 20 non-responders). The article does not give an explicit per-item denominator for Table 2 (a note about n=67-68 due to missing data applies to Table 1 demographics, not explicitly extended to Table 2), so AE_denominator is assumed = N (88).
article.SafetyReported: This article is not framed as a clinical AE/safety study — it has no dedicated safety endpoint, no CTCAE/SAE grading, and no report of medical complications, hospitalizations, or deaths, despite describing cardiac monitoring during dosing. It does report a study-specific, unvalidated 'acute subjective effects of ibogaine' Likert scale (Table 2) in which 4 of 15 items describe negative/challenging phenomenology (physical discomfort, fear, frightening images, recalling difficult memories) rather than positive/neutral effects. Per the codebook's instruction not to silently fold challenging-experience phenomenology into a null AE count, these four items were extracted as AE/challenging-experience events, so SafetyReported/AnyAEReported were coded Y. The Discussion explicitly recommends future research 'evaluate the safety of this treatment using a rigorous controlled design,' underscoring that no formal safety evaluation was conducted here.
article.NumDistinctAEs: Counted as the 4 negative/challenging items from the 15-item acute-effects scale in Table 2 (physical discomfort, fear, frightening images, difficult memories recalled); the other 11 items describe neutral or positive phenomenology (visions, insight, spirituality, bliss, etc.) and were not coded as AEs.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: Table 2 gives only per-item endorsement percentages of the full sample; the article never reports a combined count/percentage of participants endorsing >=1 of these items, so this cannot be derived without assuming independence/overlap.
article.WorstSeverity: All four extracted events defaulted to Mild under the rubric's under-specified-AE rule (no intervention, escalation, or seriousness signal reported for any of them), so WorstSeverity = Mild.
article.PctBIPOC: Table 1 reports ethnicity as a single aggregate figure: White/Caucasian 89% vs. Non-White/Other 11%; no subgroup breakdown to sum.
article.PctIndigenous: Not broken out separately from the 'Non-White/Other' aggregate in Table 1.
article.ArmScope: Single-arm naturalistic survey of ibogaine-treated patients only, with no non-exposed comparator group; the entire N=88 sample is psychedelic-exposed, so ArmScope = psychedelic_arm per the schema's guidance for single-arm cohorts/surveys.

ae_events.Davis 2017_AE01: Physical discomfort endorsed by 74% on an unvalidated, study-specific acute-effects Likert scale; no detail on nature, severity, duration, or clinical management, so severity defaulted to Mild and flagged indeterminate per the rubric's under-specified-AE rule. Onset coded in-session as the item measures 'acute subjective effects' during the ibogaine experience; the article does not distinguish which of ibogaine's multi-hour dosing phases the discomfort occurred in.
ae_events.Davis 2017_AE02: Fear endorsed by 51%; classic Barrett-CEQ-sense challenging-experience phenomenology, expected during ibogaine dosing per the rubric's core adaptation principle. No intervention need, escalation, or post-session persistence reported, so graded Mild and flagged indeterminate (only a Likert endorsement, no detail).
ae_events.Davis 2017_AE03: Frightening images endorsed by 49%; in-session perceptual/challenging-experience item on the same unvalidated scale, no further detail on intensity or consequence, graded Mild and flagged indeterminate.
ae_events.Davis 2017_AE04: Recalling/experiencing difficult memories endorsed by 36%; judgment call to include this as a challenging-experience event given its negative framing alongside the fear/frightening-images items on the same acute-effects scale, distinct from clearly positive insight/reframing items (e.g., 'gained insight into past trauma'). No distress level, duration, or intervention detail given, so graded Mild and flagged indeterminate.
